Question:
Nicolas is planning to send a package to his friend Anton, who is a stamp collector. To pay for the postage, Nicolas would like to cover the package with a large number of stamps. Suppose he has a collection of \(5\)-cent, \(10\)-cent, and \(25\)-cent stamps, with exactly \(20\) of each type. What is the greatest number of stamps Nicolas can use to make exactly \(\$7.10\) in postage?

(Note: The amount \(\$7.10\) corresponds to \(7\) dollars and \(10\) cents. One dollar is worth \(100\) cents.)
Solution:
It is easier to minimize the stamps left unused. All \(60\) stamps together are worth

\[
20(5+10+25)=800\text{ cents}.
\]

To use exactly \(710\) cents, Nicolas must leave out \(800-710=90\) cents. Leaving out as few stamps as possible will let him use as many as possible.

Three stamps can be worth at most \(3\cdot25=75\) cents, so at least four are needed. Four \(25\)-cent stamps total \(100\) cents. If even one of those is replaced by a smaller stamp, the value drops by at least \(15\) cents, to at most \(85\) cents. Thus four stamps cannot total \(90\) cents either.

Five stamps can do it:

\[
25+25+25+10+5=90.
\]

So the smallest number left unused is \(5\), and the greatest number used is \(60-5=\boxed{55}\), choice \(\boxed{\text{E}}\).

When a desired selection is close to the entire collection, counting what must be left out can turn a large maximization problem into a small one.
